q1: SELECT ITM.ITEMN, ITPV.VENDN FROM ITM ITM, (SELECT DISTINCT ITP.ITEMN, PUR.VENDN FROM ITP ITP, PUR PUR WHERE ITP.PONUM = PUR.PONUM AND PUR.ODATE > 85) ITPV WHERE ITM.ITEMN = ITPV.ITEMN AND ITM.ITEMN > 1 AND ITM.ITEMN < 20
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITM.ITEMN, PUR.VENDN FROM ITM ITM, ITP ITP, PUR PUR WHERE ITP.PONUM = PUR.PONUM AND ITM.ITEMN = ITP.ITEMN AND PUR.ODATE > 85 AND ITM.ITEMN > 1 AND ITM.ITEMN < 20
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are equivalent under the given schema. Both compute the same set of (ITEMN, VENDN) pairs for items existing in ITM with 1 < ITEMN < 20 that have at least one ITP row joining to a PUR row with PUR.ODATE > 85, with duplicates removed. Q1 removes duplicates inside the ITP–PUR subquery before joining ITM; Q2 removes duplicates after joining all three tables. Because ITM has a primary key on ITEMN (so the ITM join does not introduce multiplicity) and both queries ultimately apply DISTINCT on the same projected columns (ITEMN, VENDN), the results are identical for all databases respecting the schema.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample exists. The placement of DISTINCT (inside the ITP–PUR subquery in Q1 vs. at the top level in Q2) does not change the final set of (ITEMN, VENDN) pairs due to the primary key on ITM.ITEMN and identical filters/join conditions.

q1: SELECT Z.A, Z.B FROM R1 X, R2 Y, R2 Z WHERE X.A = Y.A AND Y.A = Z.A AND X.A = Z.A AND Y.B = Z.B
q2: SELECT Z.A, Z.B FROM R1 X, R2 Y, R2 Z WHERE X.A = Y.A AND Y.A = Z.A AND X.A = Z.A
explanation: Because R2 has PRIMARY KEY (A), the join forces Y and Z to be the same row for any matched A. Thus Y.B = Z.B is redundant except when B is NULL: in SQL, NULL = NULL evaluates to unknown (not true), so Q1 filters such rows out while Q2 keeps them.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO R2 (A, B) VALUES (1, NULL);
INSERT INTO R1 (A, B) VALUES (1, 10);
counterexample_dsp: Make R2 contain a single row with A=1 and B=NULL, and R1 contain a matching row with A=1. Q2 returns (1, NULL). Q1 applies Y.B = Z.B, which is NULL = NULL -> unknown, so it returns no rows.

q1: SELECT ITEMPRICE.NP, ITM.TYPE, ITM.ITEMNO FROM (SELECT DISTINCT ITP.ITEMNO AS ITN, ITP.NP AS NP FROM ITP ITP WHERE ITP.NP > 1000) ITEMPRICE, ITM ITM WHERE ITEMPRICE.ITN = ITM.ITEMNO
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITP.NP, ITM.TYPE, ITM.ITEMNO FROM ITP ITP, ITM ITM WHERE ITP.NP > 1000 AND ITP.ITEMNO = ITM.ITEMNO
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are equivalent under the given schema. Both return the set of (NP, TYPE, ITEMNO) for items where ITP.NP > 1000 and there exists a matching ITM row on ITEMNO. The only syntactic difference is where DISTINCT is applied: Q1 deduplicates (ITEMNO, NP) before joining; Q2 deduplicates (NP, TYPE, ITEMNO) after the join. Because ITM has a primary key on ITEMNO, TYPE is functionally determined by ITEMNO, so DISTINCT on (NP, TYPE, ITEMNO) is effectively DISTINCT on (NP, ITEMNO). Moreover, the join is one-to-one on ITEMNO, so pushing DISTINCT before/after the join does not change the result. Therefore, no counterexample exists.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample exists: with ITM.ITEMNO being a primary key, TYPE is uniquely determined by ITEMNO, making both queries return the same deduplicated set.

q1: SELECT ITM.ITEMNO, ITEMPRICE.NP FROM (SELECT DISTINCT ITP.ITEMNO AS ITN, ITP.NP AS NP FROM ITP ITP) ITEMPRICE, ITM ITM WHERE ITEMPRICE.ITN = ITM.ITEMNO
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITM.ITEMNO, ITP.NP FROM ITP ITP, ITM ITM WHERE ITP.ITEMNO = ITM.ITEMNO
explanation: Both queries compute the distinct (ITEMNO, NP) pairs from ITP that have a matching ITEMNO in ITM. Q1 applies DISTINCT to (ITEMNO, NP) before joining; Q2 joins first and then applies DISTINCT. Because ITM.ITEMNO is a primary key (one row per ITEMNO) and the join is only on ITEMNO, pushing DISTINCT across the join does not change the result. Therefore Q1 and Q2 are equivalent for all data respecting the schema.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample exists under the given schema and constraints; both queries always return the same result.

q1: SELECT * FROM ITP ITP WHERE ITP.ITEMN IN (SELECT ITL.ITEMN FROM ITL ITL WHERE ITL.WKCEN = 468 AND ITL.LOCAN = 0)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT ITP.* FROM ITP ITP, ITL ITL WHERE ITP.ITEMN = ITL.ITEMN AND ITL.WKCEN = 468 AND ITL.LOCAN = 0
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are equivalent under the given schema. Both return the set of rows from ITP whose ITEMN appears in ITL with WKCEN = 468 and LOCAN = 0. Q2’s DISTINCT does not change results because ITP.ITEMN is a primary key (so each ITP row is unique), and duplicates from joining multiple ITL rows collapse to the same single ITP row. IN vs JOIN also behaves the same here because ITP.ITEMN cannot be NULL (PRIMARY KEY), so NULL-related IN nuances don’t create divergence.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample exists under the provided constraints. To make them differ, you would need either duplicate rows in ITP with the same ITEMN (which is forbidden by the PRIMARY KEY), or allow NULL ITEMN in ITP (also forbidden by PRIMARY KEY), or remove DISTINCT in Q2.

q1: SELECT T.TMEMBER FROM DEPTS D, TEAMS T WHERE D.DPROJ = T.TPROJ AND D.DNAME = 'SECURITY'
q2: SELECT V1.E FROM (SELECT D.DNAME AS D, D.DPROJ AS P, P.EMPL AS E FROM DEPTS D, PAYROLL P WHERE D.DNAME = P.PDEPT) V1, (SELECT T.TMEMBER AS E, P.PDEPT AS D, T.TPROJ AS P FROM TEAMS T, PAYROLL P WHERE T.TMEMBER = P.EMPL) V2 WHERE V1.D = 'SECURITY' AND V1.P = V2.P AND V1.E = V2.E AND V1.D = V2.D
explanation: Q1 returns team members on projects that belong to a department whose DNAME equals the literal 'SECURITY'. Q2 additionally requires that the same employee’s payroll department (PAYROLL.PDEPT) equals that department name and matches on the same project, enforcing V1.E=V2.E, V1.P=V2.P, and V1.D=V2.D. Thus, if a team member works on the ‘SECURITY’ project but their payroll department differs from that department id, Q1 includes them while Q2 filters them out.
counterexample_dsp: Use a DEPTS row with DNAME set to 0 (so the predicate DNAME='SECURITY' is satisfied under common numeric coercion), a TEAMS row on that project, and a PAYROLL row for the same employee but with a different PDEPT (not 0). Then Q1 returns the team member; Q2 returns empty because it requires DNAME=PDEPT for the same employee.

q1: SELECT Y.* FROM PAYROLL X, APPLICANT Y WHERE X.SSNO = Y.SSNO AND X.DEPTNO = 29
q2: SELECT C.* FROM PAYROLL A, (SELECT Y.SSNO, Y.DEPTNO FROM PAYROLL Y) B, APPLICANT C WHERE A.SSNO = B.SSNO AND C.SSNO = A.SSNO AND B.DEPTNO = 29
schema:
CREATE TABLE PAYROLL (SSNO INT, DEPTNO INT);
CREATE TABLE APPLICANT (SSNO INT, JOBTITILE INT, OFFICENO INT);
explanation: Q1 joins APPLICANT with a single PAYROLL alias filtered to DEPTNO=29. Q2 self-joins PAYROLL (A and B) on SSNO, but only filters B by DEPTNO=29 while A is unfiltered; then it joins APPLICANT on SSNO. Thus, for an SSNO that has k rows in PAYROLL overall and m rows in DEPTNO=29, Q1 returns m * (#applicant rows) while Q2 returns k * m * (#applicant rows). Therefore, duplicates can differ whenever an SSNO has additional PAYROLL rows outside dept 29 (or duplicates).
counterexample_dsp: One applicant SSNO=1. PAYROLL has two rows for SSNO=1: one in DEPTNO=29 and one in DEPTNO=10. Q1 returns the applicant once (only the dept 29 row matches). Q2 returns the applicant twice because A has 2 rows for SSNO=1 and B has 1 dept-29 row, creating 2 join combinations.

q1: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP X WHERE (X.EMP, X.DEPT) IN (SELECT Y.MGR, Y.DEPT FROM DEPT Y WHERE Y.LOC = 3)
q2: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP X, DEPT Y WHERE X.DEPT = Y.DEPT AND Y.LOC = 3 AND X.EMP = Y.MGR
schema:
CREATE TABLE EMP (NAME INT, DEPT INT, EMP INT);
CREATE TABLE DEPT (DEPT INT, LOC INT, MGR INT);
explanation: Q1 uses a tuple IN predicate, which only tests existence: each EMP row that matches any DEPT row with (MGR, DEPT) and LOC=3 is returned once. Q2 performs an inner join; if multiple DEPT rows match the same EMP row (duplicate (DEPT, MGR, LOC=3) entries), Q2 returns duplicates, while Q1 does not. Hence they differ in the presence of duplicate DEPT rows.
counterexample_dsp: Create two identical DEPT rows with LOC=3 for the same (DEPT, MGR), and one EMP row whose (EMP, DEPT) matches that pair. Q1 returns one row; Q2 returns two duplicate rows.

q1: SELECT X.B AS XB FROM R X WHERE X.A = 5 AND X.C < 1
q2: SELECT X.B AS XB FROM R X WHERE X.A < 10
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT, B INT, C INT);
explanation: Q1 returns B from rows where A = 5 and C < 1. Q2 returns B from rows where A < 10, regardless of C. Therefore, Q2 is less restrictive and can include rows with A < 10 that are excluded by Q1 (e.g., A != 5, or A = 5 with C >= 1 or C IS NULL). Q1 is a subset of Q2, so they are not equivalent.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO R (A, B, C) VALUES (5, 10, 0);
INSERT INTO R (A, B, C) VALUES (7, 20, 100);
counterexample_dsp: Include one row with A=7 (A<10 but A!=5) so it appears only in Q2, and one row with A=5 and C=0 to show overlap. Q1 returns B=10; Q2 returns B=10 and B=20.

q1:
SELECT 
    P.UID,
    P.UNAME,
    COALESCE(Q.CNT, 0) AS CNT
FROM (
    SELECT X.UID, X.UNAME
    FROM USER X
    WHERE X.CITY = 3
) AS P
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT Y.UID, COUNT(*) AS CNT
    FROM PICTURE Y
    WHERE Y.SIZE > 1000000
    GROUP BY Y.UID
) AS Q
USING (UID);
q2: SELECT X.UID AS UID, X.UNAME AS UNAME, COUNT(*) AS CNT FROM USER X, PICTURE Y WHERE X.UID = Y.UID AND Y.SIZE > 1000000 AND X.CITY = 3 GROUP BY X.UID, X.UNAME
schema:
CREATE TABLE USER (UID INT, UNAME INT, CITY INT);
CREATE TABLE PICTURE (UID INT, SIZE INT);
explanation: Q1 keeps all users from CITY = 3 via a LEFT JOIN and fills missing picture counts with 0 (COALESCE). Q2 uses an INNER JOIN between USER and PICTURE filtered by SIZE > 1000000, so users without any qualifying pictures are omitted entirely. Therefore, users with zero qualifying pictures appear in Q1 with CNT = 0 but do not appear in Q2.
counterexample_dsp: Include a user in CITY = 3 who has no pictures with SIZE > 1000000 (or only smaller pictures). Q1 will return this user with CNT = 0; Q2 will return no row for this user. Also include another user with large pictures to show matching rows align.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT X.USRUID AS XID, X.USRNAME AS XNAME FROM USR X, PIC U, PIC V, PIC W WHERE X.USRUID = U.PICUID AND X.USRUID = V.PICUID AND X.USRUID = W.PICUID AND W.PICSIZE = V.PICSIZE AND U.PICSIZE < 500000 and V.PICSIZE >= 500000
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.USRUID AS XID, X.USRNAME AS XNAME FROM USR X, PIC U, PIC V WHERE X.USRUID = U.PICUID AND X.USRUID = V.PICUID AND U.PICSIZE < 500000 and V.PICSIZE >= 500000
schema:
CREATE TABLE USR (USRUID INT, USRNAME VARCHAR);
CREATE TABLE PIC (PICUID INT, PICSIZE INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are equivalent. Q2 returns users who have at least one picture with size < 500000 (U) and at least one picture with size >= 500000 (V). Q1 adds a third alias W with the condition W.PICSIZE = V.PICSIZE, but since W can be the very same row as V (self-join is allowed in SQL), this adds no extra restriction. Both queries use DISTINCT on the same projected columns, so multiplicity differences from the extra join are removed.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample exists: for any V row that satisfies V.PICSIZE >= 500000, W can be chosen equal to V, making Q1’s extra predicate always satisfiable whenever Q2’s predicates are satisfied.

q1: SELECT X.PNUM AS XP FROM PARTS X WHERE (X.PNUM, X.QOH) IN (SELECT Y.PNUM, COUNT(Y.SHIPDATE) AS CNT FROM SUPPLY Y WHERE Y.SHIPDATE < 10)
q2: SELECT X.PNUM AS XP FROM PARTS X, (SELECT Y.PNUM AS SUPPNUM, COUNT(Y.SHIPDATE) AS CT FROM SUPPLY Y WHERE Y.SHIPDATE < 10 GROUP BY Y.PNUM) TEMP WHERE X.QOH = TEMP.CT AND X.PNUM = TEMP.SUPPNUM
schema:
CREATE TABLE PARTS (PNUM INT, QOH INT);
CREATE TABLE SUPPLY (PNUM INT, SHIPDATE INT);
explanation: Q2 correctly computes, per PNUM, the number of SUPPLY rows with SHIPDATE < 10 and returns parts whose QOH equals that per-PNUM count. Q1, however, is missing a GROUP BY in its subquery: it collapses to a single row consisting of an arbitrary Y.PNUM and the global COUNT of qualifying rows across all PNUMs. Thus Q1 compares (X.PNUM, X.QOH) to a single (PNUM, total_count) pair, while Q2 compares X.QOH to the per-PNUM count for X.PNUM. They differ whenever there are multiple PNUMs with qualifying rows and no part has QOH equal to the global total.
counterexample_dsp: Make two parts whose QOH match their own per-PNUM counts, but ensure the total number of qualifying SUPPLY rows across all PNUMs is larger than any single per-PNUM count. Then Q2 returns both parts; Q1 returns none because it only matches (some PNUM, total_count) and no part has QOH = total_count.

q1: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP X WHERE (X.EMP, X.DEPT) IN (SELECT Y.MGR, Y.DEPT FROM DEPT Y WHERE Y.LOC = 3)
q2: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP X
schema:
CREATE TABLE EMP (NAME INT, DEPT INT, EMP INT);
CREATE TABLE DEPT (DEPT INT, LOC INT, MGR INT);
explanation: Q1 filters EMP to only those rows where the pair (EMP, DEPT) matches a (MGR, DEPT) pair from DEPT with LOC = 3. Q2 returns all EMP rows. They differ whenever there exists any employee whose (EMP, DEPT) does not appear among DEPT rows with LOC = 3 (or when such DEPT rows are absent). Row-value IN and the WHERE clause in Q1 perform the filtering that Q2 lacks.
counterexample_dsp: Two employees exist; only one manages a department with LOC = 3 and matching DEPT. Thus Q1 returns only the matching employee’s NAME, while Q2 returns both.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT X.X AS AX FROM A X, B Y WHERE X.YA = Y.YB
q2:
SELECT X.X AS AX
FROM A X, A Y, B Z
WHERE X.X = Y.X
  AND X.YA = Z.YB

UNION ALL

SELECT 1 AS AX
FROM A X
WHERE 1 = 0;
schema:
CREATE TABLE A (X INT, YA INT);
CREATE TABLE B (YB INT);
explanation: Q1 returns the distinct set of A.X values that have at least one matching B row where A.YA = B.YB. Q2 joins A as X with A as Y on X.X = Y.X and with B on X.YA = B.YB, without DISTINCT; this inflates multiplicities by the number of A rows sharing the same X (and any duplicates in B). The UNION ALL part adds nothing (WHERE 1=0). Hence Q1 deduplicates while Q2 can output duplicates, so they are not equivalent under bag semantics.
counterexample_dsp: Make two rows in A with the same X value, where only one of them matches a B row on YA=YB. Q1 returns X once due to DISTINCT; Q2 returns it twice because the self-join on A (X.X = Y.X) produces two rows.

q1: SELECT X.X AS AX FROM A X WHERE X.YX = 'HELLO'
q2: SELECT X.X AS AX FROM A X WHERE X.YX = 'HELLO HI'
schema: CREATE TABLE A (X INT, YA INT, YX VARCHAR);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 filter on different string literals in A.YX: Q1 matches rows where YX = 'HELLO', while Q2 matches rows where YX = 'HELLO HI'. With exact string equality and no other operations (no joins, no aggregation), they can return different rows.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO A (X, YA, YX) VALUES (1, 100, 'HELLO');
INSERT INTO A (X, YA, YX) VALUES (2, 200, 'HELLO HI');
counterexample_dsp: Include one row with YX='HELLO' and another with YX='HELLO HI'. Q1 will return the X value from the 'HELLO' row; Q2 will return the X value from the 'HELLO HI' row, producing different results.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT X.X AS X FROM R1 X, R2 Y WHERE X.Y = Y.Y AND X.X = 1
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.X AS X FROM R1 X, R1 Y, R2 Z WHERE X.X = Y.X AND X.Y = Z.Y AND X.X = 1
schema:
CREATE TABLE R1 (X INT, Y INT);
CREATE TABLE R2 (Y INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are equivalent. Both return {1} iff there exists at least one row in R1 with X=1 whose Y value appears in R2. In Q2, the extra self-join to R1 (alias Y) with condition X.X = Y.X is redundant because X.X=1 already ensures at least the X row itself satisfies the join; it does not add any filtering. DISTINCT removes any multiplicity differences.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample exists under the given schema; the additional self-join in Q2 does not change the result set compared to Q1.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT * FROM R X WHERE X.A1 = X.A2 AND X.A2 = X.A3
q2: SELECT DISTINCT * FROM R X WHERE X.A1 = X.A2 AND X.A1 = X.A3
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A1 INT, A2 INT, A3 INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are equivalent. Both predicates require two equalities to be TRUE simultaneously. In SQL's three-valued logic, if A1 = A2 is TRUE and either A2 = A3 (Q1) or A1 = A3 (Q2) is TRUE, then all three columns must be non-NULL and equal (A1 = A2 = A3). Thus both queries select exactly the rows where A1, A2, and A3 are all equal; DISTINCT does not introduce a difference. There is no data that makes one predicate TRUE and the other FALSE.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample exists: under SQL semantics (including NULL handling), both filters are satisfied iff A1, A2, and A3 are all equal and non-NULL.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT X.* FROM R X, R Y
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.* FROM R X
schema: CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
explanation: Q1 cross joins R with itself (R X, R Y) but projects only X.*, then DISTINCT collapses the multiplicity introduced by the cross join. Q2 directly returns DISTINCT rows from R. In all cases (including duplicates, NULLs, and even empty R), both yield the same set of distinct rows of R. Therefore, Q1 and Q2 are equivalent and no counterexample exists.
counterexample_dsp: No dataset can make Q1 and Q2 differ: the cross join in Q1 only multiplies rows but DISTINCT on X.* removes that effect, matching Q2’s DISTINCT over R.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT Y.A AS A FROM R X, R Y WHERE X.A = Y.A
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.A AS A FROM R X
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT);
explanation: Q1 performs a self-join on R with the condition X.A = Y.A and selects DISTINCT Y.A. Because SQL equality returns UNKNOWN for NULL = NULL, rows where A is NULL cannot satisfy the join predicate and are excluded. Q2 simply returns DISTINCT values of A from R, which includes a single NULL (DISTINCT groups NULLs). Thus, they differ in NULL handling.
counterexample: INSERT INTO R (A) VALUES (NULL);
counterexample_dsp: Include a row with A = NULL. Q1 filters it out due to the equality join, while Q2 returns NULL as a distinct value.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT Y.A1 AS A1, Y.A2 AS A2 FROM R X, R Y WHERE X.A1 = Y.A1 AND X.A2 = Y.A2
q2: SELECT DISTINCT X.A1 AS A1, X.A2 AS A2 FROM R X
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A1 INT, A2 INT);
explanation: Q1 self-joins R on equality of both columns and returns DISTINCT Y.(A1,A2). Because SQL equality comparisons with NULL evaluate to UNKNOWN (not TRUE), any row where A1 or A2 is NULL will not match even with itself and is filtered out. Q2 simply returns DISTINCT pairs from R, including rows containing NULLs. Hence they differ in the presence of NULLs.
counterexample: INSERT INTO R (A1, A2) VALUES (1, NULL);
counterexample_dsp: Insert a row where A2 is NULL. Q1’s equality join finds no matching pair (NULL = NULL is not TRUE), so it returns empty; Q2 returns the distinct row.

q1: SELECT X.A, SUM(X.A + X.B) FROM R X GROUP BY X.A
q2: SELECT Y.A, SUM(Y.A + Y.B) FROM R Y GROUP BY Y.A
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT, B INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are identical except for the table alias name (X vs Y). Both compute, for each A value in R, the sum of (A + B). There are no joins, filters, or differing functions; NULL handling is the same (A + B is NULL if either is NULL, and SUM ignores NULLs). Therefore they are equivalent under all datasets.
counterexample_dsp: No dataset can make these two queries return different results because they are syntactically and semantically the same query.

q1: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 50) Y WHERE Y.X < 200
q2: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X < 200) Y WHERE Y.X > 50
schema: CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are equivalent. Both apply the filters X > 50 and X < 200; the nesting just makes it (X > 50) AND (X < 200). AND is commutative in SQL’s three-valued logic, and rows with NULL in X fail both comparisons in both queries. No joins, aggregations, or other constructs that could cause divergence.
counterexample_dsp: No dataset will make Q1 and Q2 differ. For illustration, the following data includes values below, at, within, and above the thresholds, plus NULL; both queries return only X in (51..199).

q1: SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 50 AND X.X < 200
q2: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 50) Y WHERE Y.X < 200
schema: CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
explanation: Q1 filters R directly with X > 50 AND X < 200. Q2 first filters R with X > 50 into a derived table, then applies X < 200. There are no joins, aggregation, DISTINCT, or NULL-dependent constructs that differ between them. The two WHERE predicates are conjunctive and order-independent; duplicates are preserved in both. Therefore, Q1 and Q2 are semantically equivalent for all data under this schema.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample exists: both queries return exactly the rows where 50 < X < 200, with identical handling of NULLs (excluded) and duplicates (preserved).

q1: SELECT COUNT(*) AS A FROM R X
q2: SELECT COUNT(Y.B) FROM R Y
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT, B INT);
explanation: Q1 counts all rows in R using COUNT(*). Q2 counts only non-NULL values of column B using COUNT(B). Since COUNT(column) ignores NULLs, rows where B IS NULL are included in Q1 but excluded from Q2, causing different results.
counterexample: INSERT INTO R (A, B) VALUES (1, NULL);
counterexample_dsp: Insert at least one row where B is NULL. Then Q1 counts that row, while Q2 does not.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 50 OR X.X < 200
schema: CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
explanation: Q1’s WHERE clause (X > 50 OR X < 200) is a tautology for any non-NULL X, so Q1 returns all non-NULL rows from R with duplicates removed by DISTINCT. Q2 unions (with UNION ALL) the rows where X > 50 and where X < 200; every non-NULL X satisfies at least one branch, NULL satisfies neither. The outer DISTINCT removes duplicates created by rows that satisfy both. Thus both queries return exactly the set of non-NULL X values, deduplicated.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample exists under the given schema and standard SQL semantics: both queries return all non-NULL rows of R with duplicates removed, and exclude NULLs.

q1: SELECT DEPT.NAME AS DNAME, COUNT(*) AS C FROM DEPT AS DEPT GROUP BY DEPT.NAME HAVING DEPT.NAME = 10
q2: SELECT T2.DNAME, T2.CNT AS C FROM (SELECT DEPT0.NAME AS DNAME, COUNT(*) AS CNT FROM DEPT AS DEPT0 GROUP BY DEPT0.NAME) AS T2 WHERE T2.DNAME = 10
schema: CREATE TABLE DEPT (DEPTNO INT, NAME INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 both group DEPT rows by NAME and count rows per NAME, then filter to the group where NAME = 10. In Q1 the filter is in HAVING on the grouped column; in Q2 it’s a WHERE on the derived grouped result. Since the predicate only references the grouped column and COUNT(*) is the same in both, they are equivalent for all data.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample exists: for any dataset, both queries return the same result (either the single group for NAME=10 with its count, or no rows if none).

q1: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 0) Y WHERE Y.X > 0
q2: SELECT * FROM R X WHERE X.X > 0
schema: CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
explanation: Q1 applies the predicate X > 0 twice: once in the subquery and again in the outer query. This is redundant and does not change the result. Q2 applies the same predicate once. With table R(X INT), there are no constructs (joins, DISTINCT, aggregation, NULL-altering operations) that could cause divergence. Both queries return exactly the rows where X > 0.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample exists. For any data (including NULLs, negatives, zeros, positives, duplicates), both queries return the same multiset of rows: all rows with X > 0.

q1: SELECT * FROM A X WHERE X.C IN (SELECT Y.C FROM A Y)
q2: SELECT * FROM A X
schema: CREATE TABLE A (C INT);
explanation: Q1 is a self-semi-join using IN that retains only rows where X.C equals some Y.C in A. Because SQL uses three-valued logic, rows with X.C = NULL do not satisfy the IN predicate (NULL IN (...) is UNKNOWN and filtered out). Q2 returns all rows. Therefore, any NULL in A.C makes Q1 and Q2 differ.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO A (C) VALUES (NULL);
INSERT INTO A (C) VALUES (1);
counterexample_dsp: Include at least one row with C = NULL. Q1 will drop it due to NULL IN (...) being UNKNOWN, while Q2 will return it.

q1: SELECT X.A1 AS A1, X.A2 AS A2, Y.B1 AS B1, Y.B2 AS B2 FROM A X, B Y WHERE X.A1 = Y.B1
q2: SELECT Y.A1 AS A1, Y.A2 AS A2, X.B1 AS B1, X.B2 AS B2 FROM B X, A Y WHERE Y.A1 = X.B1
schema:
CREATE TABLE A (A1 INT, A2 INT);
CREATE TABLE B (B1 INT, B2 INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are the same inner join between A and B on A.A1 = B.B1, projecting the same four columns with identical aliases (A1, A2, B1, B2). Inner joins are commutative, and both queries preserve duplicates and handle NULLs identically (rows with NULL in join keys do not match). Therefore, they always return identical results.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample exists under the given schema and standard SQL semantics; for any data, both queries produce the same result set.

q1: SELECT * FROM R1 X, (SELECT * FROM R2 UNION ALL SELECT * FROM R3) Y
explanation: Q1 computes the cross join of R1 with (R2 UNION ALL R3). Q2 computes (R1×R2) UNION ALL (R1×R3). Because CROSS JOIN distributes over UNION ALL and all three tables have the same single INT column, both queries produce the same multiset of pairs (R1.X, R2.X/R3.X) for any data. There are no filters, no aggregations, and UNION ALL preserves duplicates identically in both forms.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample exists under the given schema; Q1 and Q2 are equivalent for all possible contents of R1, R2, and R3.

q1: SELECT X.B AS XB, Y.B AS YB FROM R1 X, R2 Y
q2: SELECT X1.XB AS XB, Y1.YB AS YB FROM (SELECT X.B AS XB FROM R1 X) X1, (SELECT Y.B AS YB FROM R2 Y) Y1
schema:
CREATE TABLE R1 (A INT, B INT);
CREATE TABLE R2 (A INT, B INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are equivalent. Q1 computes the Cartesian product of R1 and R2 and projects B from each. Q2 first projects B from each table in derived tables (without DISTINCT or filters), then computes the same Cartesian product. Since the subqueries do not change row counts or duplicates, both queries return the same multiset of (XB, YB) for any data.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample exists. For any contents of R1 and R2 (including duplicates and NULLs), both queries produce identical results.

q1: SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM R UNION ALL SELECT * FROM S) X
schema:
CREATE TABLE R (X INT);
CREATE TABLE S (X INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are equivalent. Both compute the multiset UNION ALL of table R and table S with identical projection (*), no filters, no joins, and no aggregation. Q1 just wraps the UNION ALL inside a derived table and selects * from it; Q2 performs the same UNION ALL directly. With the same schema and types, they preserve duplicates identically and handle NULLs the same. Therefore, no database instance can make their results differ.
counterexample_dsp: Not applicable — the queries are semantically identical under the given schema, so no data can trigger a difference.

q1: SELECT * FROM A X, (SELECT * FROM B Y WHERE Y.X < 100) Z WHERE X.X = Z.X
q2: SELECT * FROM A X, B Y WHERE X.X = Y.X AND Y.X < 100
schema:
CREATE TABLE A (X INT);
CREATE TABLE B (X INT);
explanation: No counterexample exists: Both queries are equivalent. Q1 joins A with a derived table Z = (B filtered by X < 100), then enforces X.X = Z.X. Q2 joins A and B and enforces both X.X = Y.X and Y.X < 100. For inner joins, pushing the filter on B into a derived table or keeping it in the WHERE clause yields the same result. NULLs and duplicates are handled identically.
counterexample_dsp: There is no data under this schema that makes Q1 and Q2 differ; both compute A ⋈ (σ B.X < 100) on A.X = B.X.

q1: SELECT X.A AS A FROM X X, Y Y WHERE X.K = Y.K
q2: SELECT X1.A AS X1A FROM (SELECT X.A AS A, X.K AS K FROM X X) X1, Y Y WHERE X1.K = Y.K
schema:
CREATE TABLE X (A INT, K INT);
CREATE TABLE Y (A INT, K INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 both perform an inner join between X and Y on X.K = Y.K and return the A values from X for matching pairs. The subquery in Q2 is a trivial projection of X(A, K) and does not change row contents or multiplicities. The only difference is the output column alias: Q1 names the column A, while Q2 names it X1A. Thus, their result schemas differ even though the row contents are the same.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO X (A, K) VALUES (1, 10);
INSERT INTO Y (A, K) VALUES (5, 10);
counterexample_dsp: Insert one matching pair so both queries return one row. The returned value is identical, but Q1’s column is named A while Q2’s column is named X1A.

q1: SELECT * FROM R1 X, (SELECT * FROM R2 Y WHERE Y.X > 0) Z
q2: SELECT * FROM R1 X, R2 Y WHERE Y.X > 0
schema:
CREATE TABLE R1 (X INT);
CREATE TABLE R2 (X INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are equivalent. In Q1, the derived table Z is just R2 filtered by Y.X > 0, and then cross-joined with R1. In Q2, R1 is cross-joined with R2 and the same filter Y.X > 0 is applied. There is no join condition involving R1 in either query, no aggregation, and the NULL/three-valued logic applies identically to the filter. Thus both return the cross join of R1 with the subset of R2 where X > 0.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample exists under this schema; both queries perform the same cross join between R1 and the filtered rows of R2 (X > 0).

q1: SELECT X.A + X.B, X.A/X.B AS A FROM R X
q2: SELECT Y.A + Y.B, Y.A/Y.B AS A FROM R Y
schema: CREATE TABLE R (A INT, B INT);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are alpha-equivalent. They both project two expressions from the same single table R: (A+B) and (A/B) (aliased as A). The only difference is the table alias name (X vs Y), which does not affect semantics. There are no joins, filters, aggregations, or differing functions. NULLs, division by zero, duplicates, and integer division behave identically in both queries. Therefore, they return the same result for every possible instance of R.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample exists because the queries are syntactically and semantically identical modulo alias renaming.

q1: SELECT * FROM A X UNION ALL SELECT * FROM A X WHERE FALSE
q2: SELECT * FROM A X
schema: CREATE TABLE A (X INT);
explanation: Q1 selects all rows from A, then UNION ALL with a second SELECT that is filtered by WHERE FALSE, which returns zero rows. Thus Q1 returns exactly the same rows as SELECT * FROM A. Q2 is simply SELECT * FROM A. There are no joins, filters (beyond FALSE), aggregations, or NULL-sensitive constructs that could diverge; UNION ALL preserves duplicates but the second branch contributes none. Therefore Q1 and Q2 are equivalent for any data.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample exists: for any contents of A (including duplicates or NULLs), both queries return exactly the same result set.

q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(C.CREDITS) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(C.CREDITS) > 10 AND COUNT(DISTINCT C.CREDITS) > 5
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(C.CREDITS) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(C.CREDITS) > 10 AND COUNT(DISTINCT C.CREDITS) > 8
explanation: Both queries aggregate courses by department after an inner join to DEPARTMENT, then filter groups by SUM(C.CREDITS) > 10 and a threshold on COUNT(DISTINCT C.CREDITS). Q1 requires > 5 distinct credit values; Q2 requires > 8. Thus, any department with sum > 10 and 6–8 distinct credit values will appear in Q1 but be filtered out by Q2.
counterexample_dsp: Create one department and six courses in it with distinct credit values 1..6 (sum=21, distinct=6). This satisfies Q1 (distinct > 5) but fails Q2 (distinct not > 8), so Q1 returns the department while Q2 returns no rows.

q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, AVG(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING AVG(I.SALARY)>50000 AND COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY)=4
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, AVG(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING AVG(I.SALARY)>50000 AND COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY)>4
explanation: Q1 and Q2 both group by department after joining Course→Department→Teaches→Instructor and aggregate over Instructor.SALARY. They differ only in the HAVING predicate on the number of distinct salaries: Q1 requires exactly 4 (COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY) = 4), while Q2 requires more than 4 (> 4). Thus a department with exactly four distinct instructor salaries (and AVG salary > 50000) will appear in Q1 but not in Q2. Join multiplicities from COURSE×TEACHES do not affect COUNT(DISTINCT) and weight each instructor salary equally in AVG when independent of instructor.
counterexample_dsp: Create one department with one course that has a taught section, and exactly four instructors in that department with distinct salaries 60000, 70000, 80000, 90000. The average is 75000 (>50000) and the distinct salary count is exactly 4. Q1 returns this department; Q2 does not.

q1: SELECT STUDENT.ID FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT NATURAL JOIN STUDENT NATURAL JOIN TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY STUDENT.ID,STUDENT.DEPT_NAME HAVING COUNT(DEPT_NAME) >= 2
q2: SELECT STUDENT.ID FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT NATURAL JOIN STUDENT NATURAL JOIN TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY STUDENT.ID HAVING COUNT(DEPT_NAME) >= 2
explanation: Both queries join COURSE, DEPARTMENT, STUDENT, TAKES, and SECTION via NATURAL JOIN, then count rows per student. Q1 groups by (STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.DEPT_NAME) and requires at least two rows within the same department for that student. Q2 groups only by STUDENT.ID and allows the two counted rows to come from different departments. Because NATURAL JOIN enforces COURSE.DEPT_NAME = DEPARTMENT.DEPT_NAME = STUDENT.DEPT_NAME (and BUILDING alignment with SECTION), a student who appears multiple times in STUDENT with the same ID but different DEPT_NAME and who takes one course in each department will satisfy Q2 (total count = 2) but not Q1 (each per-department group has count = 1).
counterexample_dsp: Student ID=1 has two STUDENT rows with different departments (10 and 20). He takes one course in each department, with matching sections/buildings. This yields two joined rows overall (Q2 passes) but only one row per (ID, DEPT_NAME) group (Q1 fails).

q1: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS = (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT WHERE TITLE='CS' GROUP BY DEPT_NAME HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT COURSE_ID)>4)
q2: SELECT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS = (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT WHERE TITLE='CS' GROUP BY DEPT_NAME HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT COURSE_ID)>4)
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are identical except that Q1 uses DISTINCT while Q2 does not. Both filter COURSE rows to those whose CREDITS equal the (single) value returned by the grouped subquery (the per-department MAX(CREDITS) over CS courses for departments having >4 distinct courses). If multiple COURSE rows from the same department satisfy that credit value, Q2 will return duplicate DEPT_NAMEs, while Q1 will collapse them to one per department. We ensure the subquery returns exactly one value (only one department qualifies), so the difference shows up solely due to DISTINCT.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO DEPARTMENT (DEPT_NAME, BUILDING, BUDGET) VALUES
  (1, 10, 100000),
  (2, 20, 200000);

-- Dept 1: 5 CS courses (qualifies), max CS credits = 4
INSERT INTO COURSE (COURSE_ID, TITLE, DEPT_NAME, CREDITS) VALUES
  (101, 'CS',   1, 3),
  (102, 'CS',   1, 4),
  (103, 'CS',   1, 2),
  (104, 'CS',   1, 4),
  (105, 'CS',   1, 1),
  -- Dept 2: fewer than 5 CS courses (does not qualify)
  (201, 'CS',   2, 3),
  (202, 'CS',   2, 2),
  -- Additional non-CS courses in dept 1 with credits=4 to create duplicates in Q2
  (106, 'MATH', 1, 4),
  (107, 'PHYS', 1, 4);
counterexample_dsp: Department 1 has 5 CS courses; its max CS credits is 4 (so the subquery yields 4). There are multiple courses in dept 1 with credits=4 (both CS and non-CS), causing Q2 to return DEPT_NAME=1 multiple times, while Q1 returns it once.

q1: SELECT STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME FROM STUDENT JOIN (SELECT TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR FROM TAKES JOIN SECTION AS S ON TAKES.COURSE_ID = S.COURSE_ID AND TAKES.SEC_ID = S.SEC_ID GROUP BY TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR HAVING COUNT(S.TIME_SLOT_ID) > 1) AS A ON STUDENT.ID = A.ID GROUP BY STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) > 2
q2: SELECT STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME FROM STUDENT JOIN (SELECT TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR FROM TAKES JOIN SECTION AS S ON TAKES.COURSE_ID = S.COURSE_ID AND TAKES.SEC_ID = S.SEC_ID GROUP BY TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR HAVING SUM(S.TIME_SLOT_ID) > 1) AS A ON STUDENT.ID = A.ID GROUP BY STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) > 2
explanation: No counterexample exists. Although Q1 and Q2 differ in the inner HAVING (COUNT vs SUM over S.TIME_SLOT_ID), the outer query groups by STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME and applies HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) > 2. Within each group, STUDENT.ID is a grouping key, so COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) is always 1 and can never be > 2. Therefore both Q1 and Q2 always return an empty result set on any database.
counterexample_dsp: Because the outer HAVING condition is unsatisfiable per group (COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) > 2 while grouping by STUDENT.ID), both queries produce no rows regardless of data. Even if the inner subqueries differ (e.g., SUM vs COUNT allowing different groups through), the final HAVING filters everything out. Hence no dataset can make their outputs differ.

q1: SELECT SUM(T) AS SU FROM (SELECT YEAR AS T FROM TEACHES NATURAL JOIN INSTRUCTOR GROUP BY YEAR, COURSE_ID HAVING COUNT(ID)>4) AS TEMP GROUP BY T
q2: SELECT SUM(T) AS SU FROM (SELECT YEAR AS T FROM TEACHES NATURAL JOIN INSTRUCTOR GROUP BY YEAR HAVING COUNT(ID)>4) AS TEMP GROUP BY T
explanation: Q1 groups by (YEAR, COURSE_ID) and keeps only those course-year groups with COUNT(ID) > 4, then sums the repeated YEAR values per qualifying course. Q2 groups only by YEAR with COUNT(ID) > 4 across all courses, producing at most one row per year. Thus, Q2 can include a year even when no single course has > 4 rows (but the year total does), while Q1 returns nothing for that year. Also, when some courses exceed 4 in a year, Q1 will multiply the year value by the number of such courses, whereas Q2 includes it once.
counterexample_dsp: Make one year (2022) have 5 joined TEACHES rows in total, split across two courses (3 for course 10, 2 for course 20). No single course exceeds 4, so Q1 returns no rows. But the total for the year is 5 (>4), so Q2 returns one row with SU = 2022.

q1: WITH S AS (SELECT ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR FROM TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR HAVING COUNT(TIME_SLOT_ID)>4) SELECT DISTINCT ID,NAME FROM S NATURAL JOIN STUDENT
q2: WITH S AS (SELECT ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR FROM TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR HAVING COUNT(TIME_SLOT_ID)>5) SELECT DISTINCT ID,NAME FROM S NATURAL JOIN STUDENT
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are identical except for the HAVING threshold: Q1 keeps groups with COUNT(TIME_SLOT_ID) > 4 (i.e., at least 5 matched TAKES–SECTION rows for a student in the same year and time slot), while Q2 requires COUNT(TIME_SLOT_ID) > 5 (at least 6). They NATURAL JOIN TAKES and SECTION on (COURSE_ID, SEC_ID, YEAR), group by (ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR), and then NATURAL JOIN with STUDENT on ID. A student with exactly 5 such rows will appear in Q1 but not in Q2.
counterexample_dsp: One student (ID=1) takes exactly 5 sections in the same year (2024) and the same time slot (7). This yields COUNT(TIME_SLOT_ID)=5 for that (ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR) group, so Q1 returns the student while Q2 returns none.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE JOIN (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) AS MAX_CREDITS FROM COURSE) AS A ON COURSE.CREDITS = A.MAX_CREDITS
q2: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE JOIN (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) AS MAX_CREDITS FROM COURSE GROUP BY DEPT_NAME) AS A ON COURSE.CREDITS = A.MAX_CREDITS
explanation: Q1 returns departments that offer a course with the global maximum credits across all courses. Q2 returns departments of any course whose credits match any department’s per-department maximum credits (the subquery loses the department key and produces just a set of credit values). Therefore, Q2 can include departments whose courses do not have the global maximum, as long as their credits equal some department’s maximum.
counterexample_dsp: Two departments with different maxima: Dept 10 has a 5-credit course (global max) and a 3-credit course; Dept 20’s max is 3. Q1 returns only Dept 10 (global max=5). Q2 returns Dept 10 and Dept 20 because 3 appears as a per-department max (for Dept 20) and thus courses with 3 credits (including in Dept 20) are included.

q1: SELECT C.NAME FROM CARRIERS AS C JOIN FLIGHTS AS F ON C.CID = F.CARRIER_ID GROUP BY C.NAME, F.YEAR, F.MONTH_ID, F.DAY_OF_MONTH HAVING COUNT(F.FID) > 1000
q2: SELECT C.NAME FROM CARRIERS AS C JOIN FLIGHTS AS F ON C.CID = F.CARRIER_ID GROUP BY C.NAME, F.DAY_OF_MONTH HAVING COUNT(C.CID) > 1000
explanation: Q1 groups by carrier name plus (year, month_id, day_of_month), so it counts flights per specific calendar date. Q2 groups only by carrier name and day_of_month, collapsing across all years and months. Because both use an inner join and count non-null columns (FID vs CID) on the joined rows, their counts per group differ only due to grouping keys. Thus, a carrier can have many flights spread across different months/years on the same day-of-month so that Q2 exceeds 1000 while each per-(year,month,day) group in Q1 stays below 1001.
counterexample_dsp: Make one carrier duplicated 32 times in CARRIERS with the same CID and NAME to amplify counts (each flight joins to 32 carrier rows). Insert 32 flights for the same day_of_month=1 but spread across different (year, month_id) pairs. Then: Q1 sees 32 per (year,month,day) group (not > 1000), so returns nothing. Q2 aggregates across months/years for that day_of_month and sees 32 flights × 32 duplicates = 1024 (> 1000), so it returns the carrier name.

q1: SELECT C.NAME FROM CARRIERS AS C JOIN FLIGHTS AS F ON C.CID = F.CARRIER_ID GROUP BY C.CID, C.NAME, F.YEAR, F.MONTH_ID, F.DAY_OF_MONTH HAVING COUNT(F.FID) > 1000
q2: SELECT C.NAME FROM CARRIERS AS C JOIN FLIGHTS AS F ON C.CID = F.CARRIER_ID GROUP BY C.NAME, F.DAY_OF_MONTH HAVING COUNT(F.FID) > 1000
explanation: Q1 counts flights per carrier per exact calendar date (grouped by CID, NAME, YEAR, MONTH_ID, DAY_OF_MONTH). Q2 counts flights grouped only by carrier NAME and DAY_OF_MONTH, collapsing across all years and months (and also across different carriers that share the same NAME). Thus Q2 can exceed the threshold by aggregating multiple months/years even when no single (carrier, Y/M/D) group in Q1 exceeds it.
counterexample_dsp: Create 1 carrier (NAME=1). Populate 32 rows in MONTHS and 32 rows in WEEKDAYS, then insert 32×32=1024 flights for that carrier, all on day_of_month=15, spread over 32 different MONTH_IDs (same YEAR). Each (CID, YEAR, MONTH_ID, DAY) has only 32 flights (<1001), so Q1 returns nothing. Q2 aggregates across all months for (NAME=1, DAY=15) to 1024 (>1000) and returns NAME=1.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT F.ORIGIN_CITY, F.DEST_CITY, F.ACTUAL_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS F JOIN (SELECT A.ORIGIN_CITY, MAX(A.ACTUAL_TIME) AS MAX_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS A GROUP BY A.ORIGIN_CITY) AS X ON F.ORIGIN_CITY = X.ORIGIN_CITY AND F.ACTUAL_TIME = X.MAX_TIME
q2: SELECT S.ORIGIN_CITY, F2.DEST_CITY, MAX(F2.ACTUAL_TIME) FROM (SELECT F1.ORIGIN_CITY, MAX(F1.ACTUAL_TIME) AS MAX_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS F1 GROUP BY F1.ORIGIN_CITY) AS S JOIN FLIGHTS AS F2 ON S.ORIGIN_CITY = F2.ORIGIN_CITY AND F2.ACTUAL_TIME = S.MAX_TIME GROUP BY S.ORIGIN_CITY, F2.DEST_CITY
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are equivalent. Both find, for each origin_city, the flight(s) whose ACTUAL_TIME equals the maximum ACTUAL_TIME from that origin, and return one row per (origin_city, dest_city) with that max time. In Q1, DISTINCT removes duplicates after joining the flights with per-origin maxima. In Q2, the join to the per-origin maxima is the same, and the subsequent GROUP BY (origin_city, dest_city) with MAX(F2.ACTUAL_TIME) is redundant because all joined rows already have ACTUAL_TIME = S.MAX_TIME. Thus both queries return the same set of tuples, including handling of duplicates and NULLs (no rows for origins where MAX is NULL due to NULL join semantics).
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample exists under standard SQL semantics for the given schema: Q1 and Q2 always produce identical results.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT F.ORIGIN_CITY, F.DEST_CITY, F.ACTUAL_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS F JOIN (SELECT A.ORIGIN_CITY, MAX(A.ACTUAL_TIME) AS MAX_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS A GROUP BY A.ORIGIN_CITY) AS X ON F.ORIGIN_CITY = X.ORIGIN_CITY AND F.ACTUAL_TIME = X.MAX_TIME
q2: SELECT P.ORIGIN_CITY, P.DEST_CITY, P.ACTUAL_TIME FROM (SELECT F1.ORIGIN_CITY, F1.DEST_CITY, F1.ACTUAL_TIME, MAX(F2.ACTUAL_TIME) AS MAX_ACTUAL_TIME FROM FLIGHTS AS F1 JOIN FLIGHTS AS F2 ON F1.ORIGIN_CITY = F2.ORIGIN_CITY GROUP BY F1.ORIGIN_CITY, F1.DEST_CITY, F1.ACTUAL_TIME) AS P WHERE P.ACTUAL_TIME = P.MAX_ACTUAL_TIME
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are equivalent. Both return all (ORIGIN_CITY, DEST_CITY, ACTUAL_TIME) rows from FLIGHTS where ACTUAL_TIME equals the maximum ACTUAL_TIME for that ORIGIN_CITY. Q1 computes MAX per origin in a subquery and joins back on (origin, max_time), using DISTINCT to remove any duplicate rows. Q2 self-joins FLIGHTS on ORIGIN_CITY, groups by the F1 row (origin, dest, time), computes MAX(F2.ACTUAL_TIME) per origin, and filters to keep only those F1 rows whose ACTUAL_TIME equals that max. Duplicates in FLIGHTS do not cause divergence because Q2’s GROUP BY collapses them just like Q1’s DISTINCT, ties are handled identically (all max-tied flights are returned), and NULLs behave the same (NULLs in ACTUAL_TIME or ORIGIN_CITY do not produce matches in either query due to SQL’s three-valued logic).
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample exists: for any data over the given schema (including duplicates and NULLs), Q1 and Q2 return the same set of rows.

q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(C.CREDITS) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(C.CREDITS)>10 AND COUNT(C.CREDITS)>5
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(C.CREDITS) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(C.CREDITS)>10 AND COUNT(C.CREDITS)>8
explanation: Both queries aggregate courses by department after an inner join with DEPARTMENT, but they differ in the HAVING threshold on COUNT(C.CREDITS): Q1 requires COUNT > 5 while Q2 requires COUNT > 8. For any department where SUM(C.CREDITS) > 10 and the number of non-NULL CREDITS rows is 6–8, Q1 will return the group and Q2 will not.
counterexample_dsp: Create a department with exactly 7 courses, each with 2 credits. The inner join keeps all 7 rows. SUM(C.CREDITS)=14 (>10) and COUNT(C.CREDITS)=7. Q1 (count > 5) returns this department; Q2 (count > 8) does not.

q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(I.SALARY)>100 AND MAX(I.SALARY)<75
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(I.SALARY)>=100 AND MAX(I.SALARY)<75
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ only in the HAVING threshold on SUM(I.SALARY): Q1 requires SUM > 100, while Q2 allows SUM >= 100. Both also require MAX(I.SALARY) < 75. Therefore, any department group where the joined instructors’ salaries sum to exactly 100 and each individual salary is below 75 will be returned by Q2 but not by Q1.
counterexample_dsp: One department with one course, and two instructors in that department with salaries 60 and 40. The join groups by the course’s department, SUM=100 (boundary), MAX=60 (<75). Q2 returns this group; Q1 does not.

q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(D.BUDGET) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(D.BUDGET)>100000 AND COUNT(D.BUDGET)>10
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(D.BUDGET) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(D.BUDGET)>100000 AND COUNT(DISTINCT D.BUDGET)>10
explanation: Both queries group by department and sum department budgets over rows produced by joining COURSE–DEPARTMENT–TEACHES. The only difference is the HAVING clause: Q1 uses COUNT(D.BUDGET) while Q2 uses COUNT(DISTINCT D.BUDGET). When the join creates many duplicate rows with the same budget value (e.g., many TEACHES rows for the same course/department), COUNT counts all rows, but COUNT(DISTINCT) counts distinct budget values only. Thus Q1 can pass the count > 10 threshold while Q2 fails.
counterexample_dsp: One department (budget = 10000), one course in that department, and 11 TEACHES rows for that course. The join yields 11 rows with the same budget value. SUM(budget)=110000 (>100000). COUNT(budget)=11 (>10) so Q1 returns the department; COUNT(DISTINCT budget)=1 (not >10) so Q2 returns nothing.

q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, AVG(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING AVG(I.SALARY)>50000 AND COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY)=4
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, AVG(I.SALARY) FROM COURSE C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) INNER JOIN INSTRUCTOR I ON (D.DEPT_NAME = I.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING AVG(I.SALARY)>50000 AND COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY)>4
explanation: Both queries join COURSE→DEPARTMENT on dept_name, COURSE→TEACHES on course_id, and DEPARTMENT→INSTRUCTOR on dept_name (note: not on instructor ID). They then group by department and compute AVG(I.SALARY) and COUNT(DISTINCT I.SALARY). The only semantic difference is the HAVING predicate on the number of distinct salaries: Q1 requires exactly 4, Q2 requires more than 4. Because instructors are joined by dept_name, all instructors of the department participate regardless of who teaches; duplicates from TEACHES do not affect COUNT(DISTINCT ...) and replicate all instructors equally, leaving AVG unchanged. Therefore, a department with exactly 4 distinct salaries (and avg > 50000) is returned by Q1 but not by Q2.
counterexample_dsp: One department with one course and one teaches row; four instructors in that department with distinct salaries 40000, 60000, 70000, 80000 (average 62500). Q1 returns the department (count distinct salaries = 4), Q2 returns nothing (requires > 4).

q1: SELECT T.SEMESTER, SUM(C.CREDITS) FROM DEPARTMENT D INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (D.BUDGET = T.YEAR + 4) INNER JOIN COURSE C ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY T.SEMESTER HAVING AVG(C.CREDITS)>2 AND COUNT(D.BUILDING)=2
q2: SELECT T.SEMESTER, SUM(C.CREDITS) FROM DEPARTMENT D INNER JOIN TEACHES T ON (D.BUDGET = T.YEAR + 4) INNER JOIN COURSE C ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) GROUP BY T.SEMESTER HAVING AVG(C.CREDITS)>2 AND COUNT(D.BUILDING)>=2
explanation: Both queries join DEPARTMENT, TEACHES, and COURSE, then group by T.SEMESTER and filter groups by two HAVING conditions. The only difference is HAVING COUNT(D.BUILDING)=2 (Q1) vs COUNT(D.BUILDING)>=2 (Q2). Therefore, any group with COUNT(D.BUILDING) >= 3 (and AVG(C.CREDITS) > 2) will be returned by Q2 but filtered out by Q1.
counterexample_dsp: Create one TEACHES row with YEAR=2016 and SEMESTER=1. Create three DEPARTMENT rows all with BUDGET=2020 (matching 2016+4) and non-null BUILDING, each with one COURSE having CREDITS=3. The join for SEMESTER=1 produces 3 rows, so COUNT(D.BUILDING)=3 and AVG(C.CREDITS)=3>2. Q1 filters it out (needs exactly 2), Q2 keeps it (>=2).

q1: SELECT ID FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT NATURAL JOIN STUDENT NATURAL JOIN TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID,DEPT_NAME HAVING COUNT(DEPT_NAME) >= 2
q2: SELECT ID FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT NATURAL JOIN STUDENT NATURAL JOIN TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID HAVING COUNT(DEPT_NAME) >= 2
explanation: Q1 groups by (ID, DEPT_NAME) and requires at least 2 rows within the same department for a given student ID. Q2 groups only by ID and counts all rows for that ID across any departments. Because the joins are NATURAL, DEPT_NAME is enforced to match across COURSE, DEPARTMENT, and STUDENT, but without key constraints the same ID can appear with multiple DEPT_NAME values (e.g., duplicate STUDENT rows with different DEPT_NAME). In that case, Q2 may return the ID (count across depts >= 2) while Q1 returns nothing (no single (ID, DEPT_NAME) group reaches 2).
counterexample_dsp: Create two departments and two courses (one per department). Insert the same student ID twice in STUDENT, each with a different DEPT_NAME. The student takes one course from each department, and matching SECTION rows exist with buildings equal to the department buildings so the NATURAL joins succeed. This yields two rows for the same ID with two different DEPT_NAME values. Q1 has two groups each with count 1 (<2), so returns nothing; Q2 aggregates both rows under the ID and returns that ID.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS = (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT WHERE TITLE='CS' GROUP BY DEPT_NAME HAVING COUNT(COURSE_ID)>2)
q2: SELECT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS = (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) FROM COURSE NATURAL JOIN DEPARTMENT WHERE TITLE='CS' GROUP BY DEPT_NAME HAVING COUNT(COURSE_ID)>2)
explanation: Q1 uses DISTINCT while Q2 does not. Both queries filter COURSE rows whose CREDITS equal a scalar value produced by the subquery (the max credits among CS courses in a single qualifying department). If multiple COURSE rows share that CREDITS value and the same DEPT_NAME, Q2 will return duplicate DEPT_NAME rows, whereas Q1 will deduplicate them.
counterexample_dsp: Make the subquery return a single scalar (one department with >2 CS courses, max credits = 4). Also add two different COURSE rows with the same DEPT_NAME and CREDITS = 4 so the outer SELECT returns duplicates. Then Q1 returns {1,2} while Q2 returns [1,2,2].

q1: SELECT STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME FROM STUDENT JOIN (SELECT TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR FROM TAKES JOIN SECTION AS S ON TAKES.COURSE_ID = S.COURSE_ID AND TAKES.SEC_ID = S.SEC_ID GROUP BY TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR HAVING COUNT(S.TIME_SLOT_ID) > 1) AS A ON STUDENT.ID = A.ID GROUP BY STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) > 2
q2: SELECT STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME FROM STUDENT JOIN (SELECT TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR FROM TAKES JOIN SECTION AS S ON TAKES.COURSE_ID = S.COURSE_ID AND TAKES.SEC_ID = S.SEC_ID GROUP BY TAKES.ID, S.TIME_SLOT_ID, S.YEAR HAVING SUM(S.TIME_SLOT_ID) > 1) AS A ON STUDENT.ID = A.ID GROUP BY STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) > 2
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ only in the inner HAVING: COUNT(S.TIME_SLOT_ID) > 1 vs SUM(S.TIME_SLOT_ID) > 1. However, both queries then group by STUDENT.ID, STUDENT.NAME and apply HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) > 2. Because STUDENT.ID is part of the GROUP BY, within any group the distinct count of STUDENT.ID is at most 1 (or 0 if NULL). Therefore the outer HAVING is never satisfied, and both queries always return an empty result set for any database. Hence no counterexample exists; they are trivially equivalent (both return no rows).
counterexample_dsp: No dataset can make the outputs differ because the outer HAVING clause (COUNT(DISTINCT STUDENT.ID) > 2) is unsatisfiable under the given GROUP BY; it filters out all rows regardless of the inner subquery’s difference.

q1: SELECT SUM(T) AS SU FROM (SELECT YEAR AS T FROM TEACHES NATURAL JOIN INSTRUCTOR GROUP BY YEAR, COURSE_ID HAVING COUNT(ID)>4) AS TEMP GROUP BY T
q2: SELECT SUM(T) AS SU FROM (SELECT YEAR AS T FROM TEACHES NATURAL JOIN INSTRUCTOR GROUP BY YEAR HAVING COUNT(ID)>4) AS TEMP GROUP BY T
explanation: Q1 groups inside by (YEAR, COURSE_ID), while Q2 groups inside by YEAR only. Thus, for a given year, Q1 produces one row per course that has more than 4 rows (count(ID) > 4), and the outer SUM(T) then effectively multiplies the year value by the number of qualifying courses. Q2 produces at most one row per year (if the total rows in that year exceed 4), so its outer SUM(T) equals just the year. Hence they diverge whenever a year has multiple courses each satisfying COUNT(ID) > 4, or when no single course does but the year total does.
counterexample_dsp: Year 2020 has two different courses (101 and 102). Each course has 5 TEACHES rows (5 instructors). Q1 will produce two inner rows T=2020 and sum to 4040, while Q2 will produce one inner row T=2020 and sum to 2020.

q1: SELECT COURSE_ID, TITLE FROM COURSE
q2: SELECT COURSE_ID, TITLE FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS > 3
explanation: Q1 returns all rows from COURSE with columns (COURSE_ID, TITLE). Q2 adds a filter WHERE CREDITS > 3, so it excludes rows with CREDITS <= 3 or NULL. Therefore, they differ whenever a COURSE has CREDITS of 3 or NULL.
counterexample_dsp: Include three COURSE rows: one with CREDITS = 4 (passes Q2), one with CREDITS = 3 (filtered out by Q2), and one with CREDITS = NULL (also filtered out by Q2 but included in Q1).

q1: SELECT DISTINCT COURSE.COURSE_ID, COURSE.TITLE, TEACHES.ID FROM COURSE JOIN TEACHES WHERE COURSE.COURSE_ID = TEACHES.COURSE_ID AND TEACHES.YEAR = 2010
q2: SELECT DISTINCT COURSE.COURSE_ID, COURSE.TITLE, TEACHES.ID FROM COURSE JOIN TEACHES WHERE COURSE.COURSE_ID >= TEACHES.COURSE_ID AND TEACHES.YEAR = 2010
explanation: Q1 joins COURSE and TEACHES only when COURSE.COURSE_ID = TEACHES.COURSE_ID (equi-join) for TEACHES.YEAR = 2010. Q2 uses COURSE.COURSE_ID >= TEACHES.COURSE_ID (inequality join), so it includes additional non-equal pairs where the course_id in COURSE is greater than the course_id in TEACHES. DISTINCT does not remove this difference because the projected rows differ.
counterexample_dsp: Create two COURSE rows with COURSE_IDs 3 and 5, and a TEACHES row for COURSE_ID 3 in 2010. Q1 returns only the equal match (course 3 with teaches 3). Q2 returns that plus an extra row pairing course 5 with teaches 3 due to the >= condition.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT INSTRUCTOR.ID, INSTRUCTOR.NAME, TEACHES.COURSE_ID FROM INSTRUCTOR LEFT OUTER JOIN TEACHES ON INSTRUCTOR.ID > TEACHES.ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT INSTRUCTOR.ID, INSTRUCTOR.NAME, TEACHES.COURSE_ID FROM INSTRUCTOR, TEACHES WHERE INSTRUCTOR.ID = TEACHES.ID
explanation: Q1 uses a LEFT OUTER JOIN with a non-equality condition (INSTRUCTOR.ID > TEACHES.ID), so it can return rows even when there is no TEACHES row with the same ID, and it can also produce rows with NULL TEACHES.COURSE_ID. Q2 is an inner equi-join (INSTRUCTOR.ID = TEACHES.ID) and only returns rows where the IDs match exactly. Thus, if an instructor’s ID is greater than some TEACHES.ID but not equal to any, Q1 returns rows while Q2 returns none.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO INSTRUCTOR (ID, NAME, SALARY, DEPT_NAME) VALUES (5, 10, 80000, 1);
INSERT INTO TEACHES (ID, COURSE_ID, SEC_ID, YEAR, SEMESTER, INSTRUCTOR) VALUES (3, 101, 1, 2024, 1, 5);
counterexample_dsp: One instructor with ID=5 and one TEACHES row with ID=3. In Q1, 5 > 3 matches and returns (5, NAME, COURSE_ID=101). In Q2, no equal ID exists, so it returns no rows.

q1: WITH S AS (SELECT ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR FROM TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT TIME_SLOT_ID)>4) SELECT DISTINCT ID,NAME FROM S NATURAL JOIN STUDENT
q2: WITH S AS (SELECT ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR FROM TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT TIME_SLOT_ID)>5) SELECT DISTINCT ID,NAME FROM S NATURAL JOIN STUDENT
explanation: Both queries are effectively identical (and always return empty) because of a logical mistake in the aggregation. In the CTE S, the rows are grouped by (ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR) and then they compute COUNT(DISTINCT TIME_SLOT_ID) within each such group. Since TIME_SLOT_ID is part of the GROUP BY key, within any group TIME_SLOT_ID is constant, so COUNT(DISTINCT TIME_SLOT_ID) is at most 1 (or 0 if NULL). Therefore the HAVING predicates (>4 in Q1, >5 in Q2) can never be satisfied. S is always empty, and the final SELECT returns no rows for both Q1 and Q2. Hence no counterexample exists.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO STUDENT (ID, NAME, DEPT_NAME, TOT_CRED) VALUES (1, 100, 10, 120);

-- Six sections in the same year with six different time slots
INSERT INTO SECTION (COURSE_ID, SEC_ID, YEAR, BUILDING, ROOM_NUMBER, TIME_SLOT_ID) VALUES
  (201, 1, 2024, 1, 101, 1),
  (202, 1, 2024, 1, 102, 2),
  (203, 1, 2024, 1, 103, 3),
  (204, 1, 2024, 1, 104, 4),
  (205, 1, 2024, 1, 105, 5),
  (206, 1, 2024, 1, 106, 6);

-- Student 1 takes all these sections
INSERT INTO TAKES (ID, COURSE_ID, SEC_ID, YEAR, GRADE) VALUES
  (1, 201, 1, 2024, 0),
  (1, 202, 1, 2024, 0),
  (1, 203, 1, 2024, 0),
  (1, 204, 1, 2024, 0),
  (1, 205, 1, 2024, 0),
  (1, 206, 1, 2024, 0);
counterexample_dsp: No dataset can make Q1 and Q2 differ because COUNT(DISTINCT TIME_SLOT_ID) within a group that already includes TIME_SLOT_ID is never greater than 1. To illustrate the issue, the following data gives a student 6 courses in distinct time slots in the same year; intuitively this might seem to satisfy a per-year count of >4, but due to the erroneous GROUP BY, both queries still return no rows.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS=(SELECT MAX(CREDITS) FROM COURSE)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE AS C JOIN (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) AS MAX_CREDITS FROM COURSE GROUP BY DEPT_NAME) AS A WHERE C.CREDITS = A.MAX_CREDITS
explanation: Q1 returns departments that have a course whose credits equal the global maximum credits across all courses. Q2 cross-joins COURSE with the set of per-department maxima (no join condition) and keeps rows where a course’s credits equal any department’s maximum. This makes Q2 effectively return all departments that have at least one course (since each department has a course with its own max), while Q1 only returns departments whose max equals the global max.
counterexample_dsp: Two departments: dept 10 has a 5-credit course (global max) and a 2-credit course; dept 20 has a 3-credit course (its own max) and a 1-credit course. Q1 returns only dept 10. Q2 returns both dept 10 and dept 20 because 3 is a per-department max (for dept 20) and Q2 matches any course with credits equal to any per-department max.
